note: Outside the stated ICP on three of five, and outside it in a way no payment structure resolves. Occupation fails outright: he is retired on Social Security, not a business owner, physician or equivalent, and the criterion was never even tested on the call because occupation was never asked — it surfaced only when he refused the price. Income fails harder than any other prospect in the batch, and not on liquidity but on structure: a stated ceiling of roughly $500 against $6,000, on a fixed income, while still supporting three daughters and maintaining a large property. Neglected health fails in the opposite direction from most of this batch: his health is not the neglected corner of an ordered life, it is the most demanding thing in it — a urologist's suspicion of prostate cancer with a declined biopsy and a September review pending, a reconstructed ACL, a damaged meniscus, a repaired retina and a hospitalisation in the last twelve months. The ICP's own wording draws the line at 'neglected, not a crisis', and this is nearer the second. Where he does fit is the part that made him easy to talk to: he is a genuinely competitive senior swimmer chasing a state qualification, which is good-to-great in its purest form, and at 165 lb swimming regularly he is the opposite of deconditioned. The finding this call contributes is the one the corpus has already flagged as the ICP's central omission — the stated definition contains no clinical criterion at all. Thomas Dixon passes the two criteria that describe capability and fails the three that describe suitability, and the criterion that should have stopped this conversation before a price was ever quoted does not exist in the ICP as written.
